On the night of 17 March 1959 the 14th Dalai Lama, then 23 years old, slipped out of his summer palace in Lhasa disguised as a soldier and fled south toward India. He crossed the border two weeks later.

China had taken control of Tibet in 1950 and 1951, and resistance had grown, first in the east. On 10 March 1959 crowds surrounded his palace in Lhasa, fearing that Chinese officials meant to seize him: this began the Tibetan uprising. On 17 March two Chinese shells landed near the palace, and that night he escaped. Days later the Chinese army shelled the palace and crushed the rising.

India's prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru gave him asylum, which strained relations between India and China. In 1960 he settled at Dharamshala in the Himalayan foothills, the seat of his government in exile. Beijing dissolved the old Ganden Phodrang government. Tens of thousands followed him into exile, the start of the Tibetan exile community.
